items.description: arXiv:2605.07155v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agnostic online learning is classically solved via a reduction to the realizable setting, utilizing Littlestone's Standard Optimal Algorithm (SOA) as a base learner. However, the SOA can be computationally intractable to implement even for a single round. To overcome this barrier, recent work in oracle-efficient online learning replaces the SOA with a realizable base learner that accesses the concept class exclusively through an offline empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. While such agnostic learners achieve expected regret $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt{T\cdot 2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$, which is near-optimal in the horizon $T$ for fixed Littlestone dimension $d_{\mathrm{LD}}$, they require $\mathcal{O}\big(T^{2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$ oracle calls. In this work, we significantly improve this oracle complexity while relying on an even weaker primitive: a weak-consistency oracle, which merely decides whether a given labeled dataset is realizable. At the core of our approach is an adaptive and dynamic agnostic-to-realizable reduction that actively prunes non-realizable label sequences on the fly. By using the VC dimension ($d_{\mathrm{VC}}$) to bound the number of dynamically maintained active paths, our algorithm reduces the total query complexity down to $\mathcal{O}(T^{d_{\mathrm{VC}}+1})$ while perfectly preserving near-optimal expected regret. Crucially, this dynamic pruning also yields a memory reduction over the standard reduction. Furthermore, we formally quantify the regret--oracle complexity tradeoff, providing upper bounds that smoothly interpolate between restricted query budgets and attainable expected regret. We complement these with lower bounds proving that any learner restricted to $Q = o(\sqrt{T})$ queries must suffer an expected regret of $\Omega(T/Q)$.

items.title: The Transformer as a Polar State Estimator
items.description: arXiv:2605.11007v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that the core components of the Transformer---attention, residual connections, normalization, and rotary encodings---arise from a single state-estimation problem. We treat each token as a noisy reading of a rotating direction on the hypersphere, taken at its own magnitude. Estimating this direction unifies the architecture: rotational dynamics give rotary encodings, robust estimation gives attention, normalization enforces the spherical geometry, and the residual connection steps toward the estimate. This reconciles normalized queries and keys with unnormalized values as opposite assumptions on whether token magnitudes are independent or share a common scale. Finally, the \emph{Polar Transformer} restores three elements standard blocks drop: rotating values alongside keys, using key magnitudes as confidence, and stepping toward the estimate rather than adding it.

items.title: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics: Observable Entropy Control under Protected-Risk Constraints
items.description: arXiv:2605.22940v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM) treats learning as an open, controlled process in which task progress, representation information, structural restrictions and externally specified risk limits jointly govern parameter updates. We characterise this mechanism through a normalised covariance-information force, metric observability and exact feasible rate constraints. The projected task rate depends on an observable cross-product that differs from the ordinary task information product when a probe set does not contain the training task. Error, finite-step and delay margins specify when admissible local requests can be implemented. A primary 288-run neural study separates information control from empirical risk protection and retains cases where extra compression worsens held-out loss. Follow-up experiments train the observable restriction in a declared 13-dimensional subspace, implement a frozen-public-encoder readout through an actual Gaussian sample channel, evaluate a fixed-coefficient sensitivity grid, and test targeted nuisance control with two-hidden-layer minibatch learning on Fashion-MNIST. The nuisance study improves shifted accuracy over ERM, while generic protected balancing accounts for most of the gain. Together, the theory and experiments identify attainable information actions, predictive costs and the separate assumptions required for population-risk certification.

items.title: Scalable Heterogeneous Graph Foundation Models for Data-Driven Optimal Power Flow in Smart Grids
items.description: arXiv:2605.23194v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast and reliable optimal power flow (OPF) approximation is important for power system operation, yet heterogeneous OPF graph models are often evaluated either with architecture-specific implementations or on limited training corpora. This paper presents a large-scale heterogeneous graph-learning workflow, built on HydraGNN, for data-driven OPF surrogate modeling and graph foundation-model (GFM) development. The workflow preserves buses, generators, loads, shunts, alternating-current (AC) lines, transformers, and device-to-bus relations and provides a common implementation for distributed preprocessing, multi-graphics-processing-unit (GPU) training, hyperparameter optimization (HPO), and downstream adaptation. Using approximately three million heterogeneous graphs from ten Power Grid Library for Benchmarking AC Optimal Power Flow Algorithms (PGLib-OPF) cases spanning 14 to 13,659 buses, we compare six heterogeneous graph neural network (GNN) families under a common HPO campaign on Frontier, resulting in two compact HeteroSAGE and HeteroHEAT models (~1.6-1.7 million parameters) that achieve the lowest observed validation MSE. Strong and weak scaling using up to 1,024 Frontier nodes show that 256 nodes (corresponding to 1,024 AMD MI250X GPUs) provides the best time-to-solution balance for the measured workload. Two downstream tasks evaluate task adaptation on the IEEE 118-bus case: a classification task to distinguish nominal operating conditions from artificially generated extreme-overload conditions and N-1 single-component-outage regression to predict bus voltage magnitude and phase angle. Partial fine-tuning provides the strongest balance between predictive performance and computational requirements.

items.title: Global linear convergence of entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient beyond tabular MDPs
items.description: arXiv:2605.24939v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the global convergence of policy gradient for infinite-horizon entropy-regularized Markov decision processes (MDPs) with continuous state and action spaces. We consider log-linear softmax policies with linear function approximation, which extend the tabular softmax parameterization while retaining a tractable policy class. Under $Q^\pi_\tau$-realizability up to a state-dependent baseline for the regularized state-action value function, we establish a non-uniform Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality for two different feature regimes. The non-uniformity arises through degeneracy of the state-averaged Fisher information matrix in the first feature regime and the uncentered feature second-moment matrix in the second. In both regimes we prove that these non-uniform constants can be bounded uniformly from below along the gradient flow. For full-affine-span features, we prove radial unboundedness of the KL regularizer and show that the state averaged smallest eigenvalue of the Fisher information matrix remains bounded below by an initialization-dependent positive constant. For simplex-valued features, we prove an analogous radial unboundedness result in the subspace orthogonal to the one vector and obtain an initialization dependent lower bound for the state averaged smallest eigenvalue of the uncentered second-moment matrix. These results imply global linear convergence of the regularized objective along the gradient flow, i.e., suboptimality decaying as $\mathcal{O}(e^{-Ct})$ for some $C>0$. Our analysis complements the global convergence theory of entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient beyond the tabular setting of Agarwal et al. (2020); Bhandari and Russo (2024); Mei et al. (2020).

items.title: A Geometric View for Understanding Concept Learning and Neuron Interpretation in Sparse Autoencoders
items.description: arXiv:2606.07007v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a unified mathematical framework for a geometric understanding of concept learning and neuron interpretation in sparse autoencoders (SAEs). While SAEs improve interpretability of neural networks by learning sparse feature representations, a principled definition of ''concept'' and ''learning'' remains unclear. We formalize concepts as sets of data points and cast concept learning as a set-alignment problem between human-defined and model-induced concepts. This formulation distinguishes three increasingly strong notions of learning -- detection, separation, and approximation -- and yields geometric conditions, error bounds, and capacity constraints for when concepts can be represented by individual neurons or multi-neuron units. It also provides a set-theoretic account for common SAE phenomena, including feature splitting, feature absorption, feature families, and hierarchical concepts. Finally, we connect concept learning and neuron interpretation through formal concept analysis, showing that the two directions need not agree and that their many-to-many structure can be organized by concept lattices. Experiments on synthetic data with ReLU and Top-$K$ SAEs illustrate the theory and reveal the effects of SAE size and sparsity on concept learning.

items.title: Sample Where You Struggle: Sharpening Base Model Reasoning via Entropy-Guided Power Sampling
items.description: arXiv:2606.09926v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sampling from the sequence-level power distribution elicits RL-level reasoning from base language models without any parameter updates, but the standard Metropolis--Hastings (MH), a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler, is both expensive and slow-mixing. We trace both to a structural mismatch: the power distribution mainly departs from the base distribution at a sparse, spatially clustered set of high-entropy decision points, yet MH proposes resampling positions uniformly along the prefix---wasting compute on near-degenerate conditionals while under-mixing precisely where modes diverge. We propose Entropy-Guided Power Sampling (EGPS), a training-free and verifier-free approximate sampler that re-derives its proposal from token-level entropy already in the forward pass. EGPS skips deterministic blocks, localizes each MCMC move to a high-entropy neighborhood, and applies Multiple-Try Metropolis at decision points---making sampling cost scale with entropy mass rather than sequence length. EGPS targets significant speedup with accuracy that matches or improves on MH power sampling: across three base models and three benchmarks it attains best or tied-best accuracy on 5 of 9 settings; on Qwen2.5-Math-7B it is best or tied-best on all three (MATH500 $75.8\%$, HumanEval $62.2\%$, GPQA $42.4\%$), with wall-clock speedups over the MH baseline of up to $12.6\times$ across these benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/hongguo7/EGPS

items.title: Anti-Collapse Dynamics and the Emergence of Multi-Time-Scale Learning in Recurrent Neural Networks
items.description: arXiv:2606.29519v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-range learning is hard for recurrent networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, because the influence of a past input fades with the lag $\ell$, and if it fades too fast the dependence cannot be learned from finite data. This fade is captured by an envelope $f(\ell)$. An exponential fade makes the data needed to learn a lag-$\ell$ dependence grow exponentially, putting long horizons out of reach; a power-law fade keeps the cost polynomial. We show that the asymptotic decay behavior of $f(\ell)$ is not fixed by the architecture. Instead, it emerges from the coupling between the state dynamics and parameter dynamics, settling into either a collapsed regime (fast, exponential forgetting) or an extended, anti-collapsed regime (slow, power-law forgetting). The intuition is a competition within these coupled dynamics. The systematic part of the training updates pulls long effective time scales back toward the network's typical range, while rare, heavy-tailed fluctuations can push a few far beyond it. When these pushes are strong enough to balance the pull, the extended regime survives. We make this mathematically precise with a coarse-grained stochastic process and derive the explicit threshold above which this balance holds. A single exponent, the spectral exponent~$\beta$, then governs both the spread of time scales and how slowly the network forgets. Realizing the regime in practice needs one more ingredient: the joint action of the architecture and the optimizer must be able to hold such a broad spread. A network whose capacity to generate broad time-scale spectra is severely constrained still collapses, even when supplied with strong heavy-tailed forcing. Heavy-tailed fluctuations thus act not as noise to be suppressed, but as the mechanism that sustains long-range learning.

items.title: Can Tabular In-Context Learners Generalize to Biomolecular Property Prediction?
items.description: arXiv:2606.31126v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting biomolecular properties from limited labeled data is a central bottleneck in protein engineering and small-molecule design. As strong pretrained encoders now supply rich fixed-length representations, the difficulty has shifted from representation learning to building a data-efficient predictor for the few-shot regime. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN and TabICL perform this prediction through in-context inference after pretraining on synthetic tables. We test whether they can act as flexible interpolators over informative fixed biomolecular representations. Treating each method as a predictor-representation pair, we evaluate across two domains. On ProteinGym, TabPFN3-ESMC600M is competitive with leading supervised-substitution entries and obtains the lowest MSE among the leaderboard-context rows considered, while Kermut remains stronger by Spearman. Performance is substantially lower under modulo and contiguous holdouts than under random splits. On the five-endpoint PpEST dataset, tabular models show favorable descriptive performance against matched supervised baselines, but the random split measures within-family interpolation and the small endpoint count precludes strong model-ordering claims. For small-molecule classification with ECFP/RDKit descriptors, no single predictor-representation pairing dominates across TDC ADMET, MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and DrugOOD, but several pairings are competitive with strong descriptor and graph baselines. Crucially, on both protein and small-molecule few-shot tasks, these predictor-representation pairs offer strong performance. We conclude that tabular foundation models can be strong biomolecular predictors, but only when coupled with expressive representations.

items.title: A Graph Signal Processing Perspective on Numerical Sequence Representations in LLM In-Context Learning
items.description: arXiv:2608.03015v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated in-context learning (ICL) capabilities for numerical inference over sequences serialized as text. Prior work has identified and characterized this form of numerical inference primarily through output-level evaluations such as prediction error. However, how numerical information is organized within LLM representations remains much less understood. To study this internal organization, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective in which attention induces a weighted graph over tokens, while token hidden states define signals on its nodes. Quantitative graph-spectral diagnostics and qualitative token-graph visualizations reveal that representations become more clearly differentiated by input dynamical complexity as context length increases. Simpler inputs produce attention-induced token graphs with stronger global connectivity and smoother, spectrally concentrated hidden-state signals, whereas more complex inputs produce more localized graphs and hidden-state signals with broader spectral support and greater high-frequency energy. These diagnostics and visualizations offer an interpretable view of the internal structure associated with numerical ICL, beyond what output-level prediction error alone reveals. Together, these findings point to systematic, context-dependent internal signatures associated with numerical ICL that are qualitatively conserved across model families.

items.title: ED-DiT: Physics-Guided Diffusion Pretraining for Transferable Molecular Representations from Electron Density
items.description: arXiv:2608.03260v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretraining has shown strong potential for learning transferable representations, yet it remains underexplored for electron-density-based molecular learning. Electron density provides a continuous three-dimensional description of molecular electronic structure, capturing both local spatial patterns and global physical quantities. This raises a key question: can electron-density fields be used for self-supervised pretraining to learn a shared representation that transfers across diverse electronic-structure-related tasks? We propose ED-DiT, a physics-guided Diffusion Transformer for self-supervised pretraining on electron-density point clouds. ED-DiT learns reusable representations by reconstructing corrupted and partially masked log-density fields across diffusion noise levels. An electron-number consistency constraint is further introduced to preserve the total electronic mass. The pretrained encoder can be adapted to property prediction, open-/closed-shell classification, molecule-electron-density retrieval, and molecule-conditioned electron-density prediction. Experiments on six EDBench tasks show that ED-DiT consistently outperforms the same architecture trained from scratch, especially under limited supervision. For molecule-conditioned electron-density prediction, it reduces RMSE from 2.2474 to 1.3753 and surpasses the available baseline. With only 10% labels, it improves orbital energy prediction RMSE from 0.0293 to 0.0138. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of physics-guided electron-density pretraining for learning transferable molecular representations.

items.title: CrevasseSeg: A Label-Efficient UAV Crevasse Segmentation Framework
items.description: arXiv:2608.15790v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Crevasse mapping from uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery supports glaciological research and field safety, but pixel-level annotation requires costly expert effort. We introduce CrevasseSeg, a binary segmentation evaluation framework from the terminus of Borebreen, Svalbard, comprising 2,244 unlabelled UAV orthomosaic tiles for self-supervised/unsupervised fine-tuning and 200 labelled tiles (24 validation, 176 test). We benchmark five self-supervised objectives (BYOL, Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD), Barlow Twins, VICReg and a combined BYOL-JSD) across O-Net, O-Net++ and a DINOv3-initialised O-Net. Frozen features are read out with a linear probe and an XGBoost classifier, both fit only on the 24 validation tiles. At the final decoder block, the two readouts invert. DINOv3 models are mostly the weakest under linear probing, often collapsing to a constant prediction, yet they are the strongest under XGBoost. This pattern does not hold at earlier decoder blocks. UMAP suggests why: DINOv3 fragments pixels into many small, locally interleaved clusters, whereas the convolutional models embed them on a single class-sorted manifold. Satellite-pretrained DINOv3 beats natural-image initialisation for every objective under XGBoost (+9.7 mDSC on average), but not consistently under linear probing. Our pipeline, DINOv3-ViT-L-Sat-O-Net-BYOL-JSD, reaches 74.75 mDSC / 61.16 mIoU (77.04 / 64.28 with a decoder-block ensemble), on par with BYOL alone, and outperforms RGB-pixel ML baselines. However, a frozen DINOv3-Sat encoder with an XGBoost readout alone reaches 77.18 / 64.17. It matches or exceeds every SSL variant and comes within 0.71 mDSC of a fully supervised DINOv3 U-Net, highlighting satellite foundation models as a strong baseline. We release CrevasseSeg as a benchmark for label-efficient segmentation in remote sensing.

items.title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Beyond $1/e$ with Feasible Gradient Queries
items.description: arXiv:2609.02145v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ when gradients may be queried only at feasible points. The online approximation coefficients $4/9$ (Aggarwal and Lu) and $2\sqrt{3}-3\approx 0.4641$ (Aggarwal and Du) rely on queries along chains that start from the all-ones vector and leave $K$. With every query in $K$, the best known coefficient was $1/e$. We give an online algorithm with coefficient $0.4013$ that, in each round, plays a random action, queries one gradient at a point of $K$, and makes one projection. Its expected approximate regret is $O(RB(1+R)\sqrt{T})$, where $R\le\sqrt{d}$ bounds the norm of points of $K$ and $B$ bounds the gradient norm on $K$. For a budget $\sum_i x_i\le k$, the bound is $O(kB\sqrt{T})$. The algorithm keeps a state $x\in K$, and the analysis applies the coordinate-chain comparison of Aggarwal and Lu inside the box $[0,x]$, which keeps every query feasible. A second comparison, along a path from $0$ in the direction $x$, cancels the extra terms that the box creates. Because the queries are feasible, they can be played, which gives regret $O(T^{2/3})$ under semi-bandit feedback and $O(T^{4/5})$ under bandit feedback with bounded values. Unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded second moment keep the $\sqrt{T}$ rate, and on a fixed function the algorithm attains $0.4013\,\mathrm{OPT}-\varepsilon$ in expectation with $O(1+R^2(1+R)^2B^2/\varepsilon^2)$ feasible gradient queries.

items.title: Reification as a Transferable Vocabulary: Zero-Shot Link Prediction with Vanilla GNNs
items.description: arXiv:2609.11347v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge graph foundation models such as ULTRA achieve zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs through dedicated architectures that hard-code a transfer mechanism. In this work we move that mechanism out of the architecture and into the representation, by \emph{reifying} the input graph: every fact becomes a node, connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations, with relation types as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. On this representation, five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and with mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN), each trained on a single knowledge graph of 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100, transfer zero-shot to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. The best of them, an off-the-shelf GAT, matches ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model pretrained on three graphs, across ULTRA's own evaluation suite. The same fixed vocabulary extends to relational databases, a row becoming an entity and a foreign-key column a relation type; a preliminary probe on two unseen databases, with no cell values, schema text or in-context labels, shows a model of this family pretrained on three knowledge graphs ranking foreign-key targets far above random-initialization and degree controls. We release the code, the checkpoints, and the evaluation pipeline for all 40 benchmarks.

items.title: Tabby: An Open Pretraining Recipe for Time Series Foundation Models
items.description: arXiv:2609.13956v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this report, we release Tabby, a long context probabilistic time series foundation model, together with a complete and open recipe of how it was built. Tabby adopts an encoder-only patch Transformer architecture and concentrates the contributions on the data and the training procedure. The pretraining corpus combines an extended real-world collection, GIFT-Eval-Pretrain+ and BLAST, with synthetic data from KernelSynth and CauKerV2, an online generator that composes temporal dynamics through randomly sampled structural causal models. Training couples a progressive convergence schedule, which yields reusable intermediate checkpoints, with a deep quantile supervision objective for intermediate layers. The resulting 145M parameter backbone supports contexts of up to 8,192 observations and serves forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, while a prompt-tuning module further improves in-distribution forecasting performance with the pretrained weights frozen. Tabby achieves competitive zero-shot forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval and the out-of-distribution TIME benchmark, while the same pretrained backbone also supports classification on the UCR Archive and zero-shot anomaly detection on TSB-AD-U. We release training pipeline and model as open source at huawei-noah/trustworthyAI.

items.title: LSTM-UT and Bounded Gated Memory for Looped Transformers
items.description: arXiv:2609.19521v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can the loop of a looped Transformer serve as a rollout, with one application of the shared block per step of a dynamical system? We started with two existing designs, one that carries only its residual stream and one, CoTFormer, that also caches every earlier state. On Rule 30, a chaotic cellular automaton, both lose the computation shortly after their trained depth. LSTM-UT, which adds an LSTM-style gated cell, does not, and it recalls earlier states better. Taking it apart shows that each ability has a simpler source. For rollouts it is decay: a fixed decay on the plain model's stream is sufficient. For recall it is an input-dependent gate: at the longest horizon a gated stream with no cell recalls as well as LSTM-UT, and no fixed decay helps. The two do not simply add, since a gated stream with a fixed decay does neither reliably. Storing every earlier state hurts extrapolation, where CoTFormer fits and rolls out further with its cache cut to the most recent repeat; in recall, the stored copy is looked up at the shortest horizon and not at the next. LSTM-UT, whose forget gate makes the decay itself input-dependent, is the only model in the leading group on both. The forget gate was added to the LSTM so that a state carried at weight one could be reset instead of accumulating; we find the same need over depth. In language modelling LSTM-UT is competitive with CoTFormer at lower training cost. Code is available at https://github.com/arskvnc22/lstm-ut

items.title: Relative Discharge Stage Classification from Battery Sensor Measurements in Laboratory Discharge Tests
items.description: arXiv:2609.27986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Relative discharge stage (RDS) is an ordinal target obtained by dividing the realized remaining discharge time by the total duration of the same discharge episode and assigning the ratio to a bin. We investigate whether these bins can be predicted from measurements available up to the present sample. The framework combines an electrothermal equivalent-circuit model and adaptive extended Kalman filter to estimate state of charge (SOC), then classifies discharge stage using the estimated SOC, current, terminal voltage, and surface temperature. With the evaluated two-layer convolutional network, the final-time prediction directly uses the three most recent observations. Earlier measurements can influence the output through the recursive SOC estimate. On complete discharge tests, the five-stage classifier achieved accuracies of 95.38% and 81.23% for FTP-75 and PDMHC and 76.41% and 73.87% for LCO_5 and LCO_6, respectively. These results characterize classification within the laboratory protocols. Incremental value over SOC alone, reference-based SOC accuracy, and utility in vehicle operation remain to be established.

items.title: Even Sharper Bounds for Transductive Learning and Its Applications
items.description: arXiv:2609.28459v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Sharper Transductive Local Complexity (STLC) as a new tool for improving current transductive bounds. Although Local Rademacher Complexity (LRC) has been used to obtain sharp inductive generalization bounds and local-complexity-based transductive bounds, it has remained open whether a localized Rademacher-complexity framework can achieve the same fixed-point and confidence structure as its inductive counterpart. STLC provides an affirmative answer to this question. STLC is constructed by first deriving a new Bernstein-type concentration inequality for the test-train process, under uniform sampling without replacement. The proof uses a new two-parameter entropy argument based on the modified log-Sobolev inequality for the swap walk. A subsequent peeling strategy with a surrogate localization functional yields transductive excess-risk bounds that match the fixed-point and confidence structure of the classical LRC-based inductive bounds without the additional logarithmic confidence gap in existing works. We further advance transductive learning through two applications. First, for realizable transductive learning over a binary-valued class of VC dimension $2\le d <\infty$ with $u\ge m\ge d$, where $u$ and $m$ are the test and training sizes, STLC gives the upper bound $O(d\log(me/d)/m}$. This rate matches the classical LRC-based, standard ERM-style inductive upper bound. It remains a logarithmic factor $\log(me/d)$ above both the optimal realizable inductive PAC rate and the transductive minimax lower bound, which are of order $d/m$. Our prior work achieves the excess risk of $O(d/m)$ in a transductive setup by randomized learning. Second, STLC gives a sharper, spectrum-adaptive excess-risk bound for transductive kernel learning than the prior local-complexity-based result.

items.title: Policy Iteration Is Not Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy
items.description: arXiv:2609.40147v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish exponential iteration lower bounds in the number of states for Howard's policy iteration on deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs), with a constant number of actions per state. This rules out polynomial-time complexity of Howard's policy iteration in both settings. We further prove that a Dantzig counterpart of Howard's policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with the known strongly polynomial bound for Dantzig's rule on deterministic discounted MDPs, these results establish an exponential separation between the two algorithms in both settings. This separation between Howard's decentralized and simultaneous selfish improvements and Dantzig's coordinated selection of a single action with the largest improvement across all states reveals a "price" of algorithmic anarchy.

items.title: SLIM: Simplex-Lattice Interpolation Merging
items.description: arXiv:2610.01037v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimizing merging coefficients for large language models can require many costly benchmark evaluations. We propose Simplex-Lattice Interpolation Merging (SLIM), which constructs a quadratic surrogate of aggregate performance on the coefficient simplex using a classical mixture design. Evaluations of individual experts and equal-weight pairs determine the surrogate with the minimum number of measurements needed to identify a general quadratic on this domain. SLIM then optimizes the surrogate without further target-metric evaluations. Experiments on two model architectures demonstrate accurate prediction of unseen multi-expert mixtures and competitive merge performance under limited evaluation budgets. Matched-budget comparisons show that structured evaluation points improve prediction fidelity over random designs, including those using regularized fitting.

items.title: Amortized Counterfactual Prediction with Graph Neural Networks
items.description: arXiv:2610.13724v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Counterfactual inference asks how an observed outcome might have differed under different circumstances, such as whether a patient would have recovered had they received a different treatment. Such questions arise whenever decisions depend on the outcomes of alternatives that were not observed. Answering counterfactual queries generally requires knowledge of the underlying causal structure, which is often unavailable in practice. A common approach is therefore to first estimate the causal graph from observational data and then perform counterfactual inference. However, errors in the estimated causal graph can propagate to downstream counterfactual predictions. To address this challenge, we introduce the Counterfactual Graph Neural Process (CFGNP), an end-to-end approach that answers counterfactual queries directly from observational data without first estimating a causal graph. CFGNP uses Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit the dual-graph structure by restricting cross-world message passing to corresponding factual--counterfactual variables. CFGNP both offers an approach that does not require knowledge of the causal graph and achieves stronger predictive performance than existing approaches. When trained on counterfactual pairs from the same structural causal model used for testing, CFGNP achieves $1.6-7 \times$ lower MSE than baselines that receive the true causal graph and the same counterfactual supervision, across seven benchmark variants. Furthermore, on synthetic causal graphs, a model trained only on 10-node graphs maintains strong predictive performance on graphs with up to 30 nodes, without retraining.

items.title: A Geometric Perspective on Reward Function Updates in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.14041v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved using Lagrangian optimisation, by jointly optimising a primal-dual problem with gradient descent to obtain the optimal reward function parameters and corresponding optimal policy. While this algorithmic view of IRL has been highly influential, gradient-based reward updates only paint a partial picture, largely ignoring the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. In this paper, we present an occupancy-space view of reward updates in IRL. We leverage the insight that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, and show that the geometry along the e-geodesic (straight line in occupancy space) toward the optimal occupancy directly affects the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space. This perspective naturally suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. We show that this preconditioned gradient is just a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward, yielding efficient natural-gradient-style updates with little additional computational overhead. We then analyse these occupancy-space reward updates from a Mirror Descent (MD) perspective, and show that policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy. Finally, we conclude with convergence results of such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.

items.title: Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.14998v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tabular foundation models predict unlabelled rows from labelled rows in a single forward pass via in-context learning (ICL). Like language models, these architectures have scaled by stacking transformer blocks, each with its own parameters. However, this approach couples compute with model size: increasing computation requires increasing the parameter count. In this work, we investigate whether tabular ICL requires distinct parameters at every block, or simply sufficient depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, a looped tabular foundation model built on the TabICLv2 architecture. Instead of stacking unique blocks, Tab-Loop takes a small set of blocks with shared parameters and applies them repeatedly in a loop during its ICL stage. We evaluate this design against standard architectures under equal training and inference compute budgets. Our experiments show that depth, rather than unique parameters, drives performance. Across classification and regression tasks on held-out synthetic tables, the TabArena and TALENT benchmarks, Tab-Loop matches the accuracy of a standard model with three times as many ICL blocks while using roughly 60% fewer parameters. Conversely, a non-looped baseline of the same size as Tab-Loop underperforms it, even when trained on 32% more tables. This pattern holds consistently whether we vary the number of distinct blocks from one to twelve or the effective depth. Furthermore, running additional loops at inference improves predictive accuracy without retraining. Training the model with deeper loops extends the range over which these extra inference steps remain beneficial, eventually matching the released TabICLv2 on TabArena at 2.7 times the ICL compute. These results show that tabular foundation models can scale their compute independently of parameter count, pointing to test-time compute scaling as a practical path toward efficient tabular models.

items.title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.21230v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all four base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.

items.title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
items.description: arXiv:2610.28709v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. Each constituent is embedded with a chemistry-pretrained transformer language model, ChemBERTa. In our proposed method, training data are produced by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy pipeline using the radiation source at 30, 80, 100, and 120 kV tube voltages over polyethylene-based shielding composite slabs of thicknesses spanning 0.15-2.5 mm. After preprocessing, the dataset contains $n = 4697$ simulated configurations on which a leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation is performed, attaining mean squared error MSE = $(1.12 \pm 0.56)\times10^{-4}$, normalized-MSE percentage NMSE% = 0.0294% $\pm$ 0.0147%, and $R^2 = 0.9988$. The corresponding per-sample percentage errors give an alpha-trimmed ($\alpha = 0.10$) absolute percentage error (APE) of 1.66% and a median APE of 1.15%. Our model's inference is several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying Monte Carlo simulation (sub-millisecond per query vs. several hours for the reference run) with effective accuracy in predicting $I(t)/I_0$.

items.title: Conditional Flow Models Convert Epistemic Uncertainty into Apparent Aleatoric Variance
items.description: arXiv:2610.29172v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly being used in place of deterministic predictors across machine learning, including for tasks that were classically formulated as regression. Given their success in such tasks, we ask the question: what useful information do the conditional distributions produced by CFMs carry beyond what a point predictor would provide? We identify a systematic phenomenon: in many natural regimes, CFM samples routinely have larger variance than the true conditional distribution, even in nearly deterministic regression problems. This effect is most pronounced where the model has not resolved the dependence on the conditioning variable, and thus the additional variance can be viewed as converting \emph{epistemic uncertainty} in fitting the ground truth conditional distribution into apparent \emph{aleatoric variance} in the generated samples. Through controlled synthetic and real-data experiments, and comparisons with explicit smoothing estimators, we show that the induced variance tracks model underfitting of complex or hard-to-fit targets, and decreases with additional training or data. We uncover surprising structure in this excess conditional variance that seems unique to CFMs and absent in the other standard probabilistic models that we test. We provide a theoretical account of the phenomenon in a simplified setting and demonstrate a consequent practical use-case of conditional flow-matching: designing high-coverage predictive sets that cover the ground-truth regression target.

items.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
items.description: arXiv:2610.31981v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recent extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We derive a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error by a residual term that vanishes under compatibility. On compact manifolds, we show that existing compatible objectives put density on infeasible velocities. To tackle both issues, we propose an exponential family over endpoints with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. In practice, and with low overhead, this reduces to a reweighting of the flow matching loss. On spaces of constant curvature, this treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Compared to prior art, our method finds the correct velocities on the test case, outperforms in general on high-dimensional product tori, and, for two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere, achieves substantial NLL improvements. When evaluated on a large dataset of human poses, our method surpasses prior work according to sample-based metrics.

items.title: Gaussian Approximation for Composition and Subsampling of Differentially Private Algorithms
items.description: arXiv:2610.33333v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The privacy analysis of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) relies on bounds for composition of subsampled mechanisms. Its privacy is bounded by that of a pair of product distributions, whose privacy loss is a sum of independent terms and has been analyzed via a variety of concentration results. Yet, existing closed-form bounds either lose a logarithmic factor or require restrictive conditions on the noise scale. Further, while sums of independent random variables are approximately Gaussian, existing CLT-based techniques give an approximation with a large error in $\delta$. We show that the privacy loss of any composition is close to a Gaussian random variable with the same mean and variance as long as each step has a small privacy loss except with small probability. Specifically, the privacy profile is bounded from above and from below by that of the Gaussian, up to an additive error $\beta$ in $\delta$ and a shift of $\varepsilon$ that grows only as $\ln(1/\beta)$. This shift does not depend on the number of steps, and thus the composition typically satisfies Gaussian differential privacy up to lower-order shifts. For $t$ steps of a mechanism with Poisson subsampling at rate $\lambda$, the variance of the Gaussian is essentially $t\lambda^2$ times the $\chi^2$ divergence of its dominating pair. This gives a new simple analysis of subsampled composition. We extend it to random allocation (balls-and-bins sampling). For the Gaussian mechanism with either sampling method at rate $1/t$, we obtain the central limit rate for $\sigma\gtrsim\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/\ln(t)$, whereas the standard R\'enyi-divergence analyses of Poisson subsampling need $\sigma\gtrsim\sqrt{t\ln(1/\delta)}/\ln(t)$. We also show that for bounded privacy losses the approximation explains the high accuracy of the connect-the-dots discretization of privacy loss distributions.

items.title: Best Policy Tracking in Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.34501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning commonly exhibits non-monotonic performance dynamics in single-task settings. During learning, a sequence of policies is generated whose true performance is unknown and may oscillate significantly across iterations. Despite this well-known phenomenon, standard experimental practice typically reports either the final visited policy or the best among periodically evaluated ones, implicitly assuming that these selection criteria reliably approximate the best-performing policy visited throughout the entire sequence. In this work, we present an empirical study on the implications of non-monotonicity for policy selection in single-task policy-based reinforcement learning. We introduce post-hoc diagnostic metrics to characterize performance degradation and assess the accuracy and efficiency of different selection criteria. These metrics allow us to evaluate commonly used selection strategies across standard continuous-control benchmarks using a well-established on-policy actor-critic method. Our results show that, in this representative experimental setting, widely adopted selection practices can deviate considerably from the best policy encountered during learning, leading to underperforming estimates and suboptimal use of computational resources. As an alternative, we recommend a validation-based policy selection strategy constrained by computational cost, which provides a more consistent and accurate approximation of the best visited policy while improving selection efficiency. Overall, our findings highlight policy selection as an underexplored factor in the evaluation protocols of reinforcement learning and motivate further study on explicit and standardized validation-based selection procedures.

items.title: InterQ-RL: Interaction-Aware Correction of Execution Mismatch in Quantized Agentic RL
items.description: arXiv:2610.35303v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-turn agent reinforcement learning (RL) relies on long closed-loop rollouts, making generation and KV-cache costs a major bottleneck. Quantized rollout reduces these costs, but its low-precision executor also serves as the behavior policy and can induce execution mismatch with the learner. Existing quantized-RL methods are designed primarily for single-turn generation. They align the learner forward with quantized rollout or correct the current-token rollout-learner ratio, without modeling the policy history that produces each agent state. Even after quantization alignment, residual rollout-learner mismatch accumulates along the state-reaching policy history, so a current action may look locally aligned despite a mismatched history. We introduce InterQ-RL (Interaction-aware Quantized Reinforcement Learning) to correct this post-alignment mismatch. It applies bounded execution-prefix correction over the state-reaching policy history, allocates correction strength across action segments by effective support under a fixed displacement budget, and requires no additional model forward pass. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbones from 4B to 30B on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, with all quantized arms sharing the same rollout with 8-bit weights, activations, and KV cache (W8A8-KV8). Across four environment-backbone settings, InterQ-RL achieves the strongest quantized endpoint result, matching BF16 to within 0.7 points and exceeding it in two settings. It matches or exceeds the learning speed of alignment alone while avoiding its late performance regression.

items.title: When does off-block Hessian curvature help an optimization step?
items.description: arXiv:2611.01335v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Testing an off-block Hessian correction alone can discard a step that lowers minibatch loss. We measure both the missed improvement and the gain from rescaling the remaining correction. A reference based on diagonal-block norms distinguishes changes in the diagonal profile during training from changes in relative off-block mass. This reference sharply bounds the off-block fraction for positive semidefinite matrices. Regrouping fixed ResNet-18 weights from stages to layers takes the estimated fraction from below to above its partition-specific bound in all six CIFAR-100 comparisons under a conditional probe screen. At nine ResNet-50 checkpoints on Stanford Cars, we measure the off-block contribution to the linearized gradient change along a K-FAC step. At four base-step endpoints, predicted and measured slopes along the original correction have opposite signs. Each subspace draw (two per checkpoint) supplies one Hessian-informed map for the off-block residual, the remainder and their sum. At unit scale before acceptance, the off-block correction alone worsens the base in 17/18 comparisons; the combination beats the remainder in ten, including nine of those 17. At one checkpoint only the combination improves on the base in both draws. Matching correction norms reverses seven of the ten preferences, including both at that checkpoint.

items.title: Same behavior, different mechanism: what finite experiments can certify about how a network computes
items.description: arXiv:2611.08469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interpretability research, AI audits and assessments of machine consciousness make claims about how a system computes, not what it outputs. We give such claims a measurement theory. A claim is certifiable from finite interventions exactly when the mechanism lies at positive information distance from those that falsify it; it then costs at least log(1/alpha) over that distance, and an adaptive experiment attains this price asymptotically. Access, geometry and the logical form of the claim set the distance. In solvable networks, behavior carries no evidence about integrated information, and quantities that select one thing and report another have cliffs beside which cost grows as the inverse square of distance, whatever the margin. Equally accurate networks implement different circuits. In language models of up to 7.6 billion parameters, 220 of 223 audited claims about circuits, and a refusal mechanism, were certified on live interventions, 89% within the cost range registered beforehand.

items.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
items.description: arXiv:2611.12491v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

items.title: A Cardiorespiratory Foundation Model Pretrained on Ten Physiological Signals for Perioperative and Critical Care
items.description: arXiv:2611.15004v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Arterial, venous, pulmonary artery, and intracranial pressures and ventilator waveforms guide decisions in operating rooms and intensive care units, yet foundation models for physiological waveforms rely almost entirely on the electrocardiogram and photoplethysmogram. We present the CArdio-Respiratory Multi-modal ENcoder (CARMEN), a single encoder pretrained without labels on ten cardiorespiratory waveforms (2.27 million modality-hours). CARMEN accepts any combination of co-recorded signals at variable lengths. A conditioning mechanism, LSCNorm, restores the absolute signal level removed by normalization; in a matched ablation, replacing it with standard normalization lowered the AUROC for intraoperative hypotension by 0.11. Across 19 tasks from Korean and US cohorts, the frozen encoder significantly outperformed both supervised models in 12 of the 15 tasks on which they were evaluated. It outperformed three pretrained foundation models on 14--17 of 19 tasks, and none of them exceeded it on any task. Given the electrocardiogram or photoplethysmogram alone, it matched or exceeded the signal-specific foundation models in most comparisons, and the performance was largely preserved even after removing the secondary channels.

items.title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2611.18043v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.

items.title: Improving fine-grained expressivity of graph neural networks
items.description: arXiv:2611.20020v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This thesis investigates the expressive power of neural networks for structured data, focusing on graph neural networks and symmetry-aware architectures. We present four main contributions. First, we characterize the generic expressive power of geometric message-passing neural networks on sparse graphs and introduce EGenNet, an architecture achieving the corresponding guarantees. Second, we use representation theory to characterize linear layers equivariant to multiple permutations, including wreath-product symmetries. Third, we study permutation-invariant set representations that preserve containment, establish dimensional bounds and impossibility results, and introduce MASNet. Finally, we propose FSW-GNN, a message-passing architecture combining strong expressivity and bi-Lipschitz stability guarantees with strong empirical performance on long-range graph-learning tasks. Together, these results provide a broader understanding of how neural architectures can preserve the geometric, algebraic, order-theoretic, and metric structure of their inputs.

items.title: Escaping Latent Traps by Remembering: Training-Free Episodic Kernel Repulsion for World-Model Planning
items.description: arXiv:2611.22470v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. Because this distance is not geodesic, it creates latent traps---local minima or flat basins behind walls, at corners and in dead ends---where memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free, test-time cost term that penalises candidate plans via a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, normalised by the current batch base cost so a single strength transfers across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR improves success in all eight settings without changing the model, planner or search budget, matching or exceeding $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute in seven of eight settings while adding $\sim 25$ ms ($<1\%$) per replan. Controlled trap-fork interventions confirm that the memory causes escape, and an untuned configuration transfers directly to DINO-WM with CEM (e.g. $44.7\%\to 100.0\%$ on long PointMaze, $+19.3$ points on long Wall) and to JEPA-WM on Metaworld mw-reach-wall ($25.3\%\to 40.7\%$).

items.title: Physics-Constrained Neural ODEs for Learning Traffic Dynamics and Trajectories from Road Entry/Exit Times
items.description: arXiv:2611.30577v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the problem of learning microscopic traffic dynamics and reconstructing vehicle trajectories from section entry/exit timestamps (EET) recorded by cameras and from the positions of a probe vehicle leading the platoon. The dynamics are difficult to recover as each vehicle's position is measured only at two points, and its trajectory between them is unknown. By combining Neural ODEs with a local density approximation, we learn a follow-the-leader model whose speed--density relation is a neural network. With such sparse data, an unconstrained network may learn physically unrealistic relations, such as negative speeds or non-zero speeds on a fully congested road. We therefore introduce a normalization that, applied to a monotone neural network with a learned regime change, enforces the endpoint conditions, guaranteeing an admissible speed--density relation while provably retaining the ability to approximate any admissible one. We validate the method on first- and second-order simulations, recovering the speed--density relation of the first-order model and reconstructing the trajectories of both models, with mean maximum position errors of 2.50~m and 2.51~m, respectively, on a 125~m road segment. On real-world ring-road data, the proposed model still yields an admissible relation, whereas both baselines violate the constraints; the large spread in the data, however, highlights the limitations of a first-order model with homogeneous driver behaviors.

items.title: A Fused Gaussian Process Bandit Framework for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2611.32092v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used to maximize expensive black-box functions when direct evaluation is costly. In many real-world applications, the high-fidelity objective can be approximated by a series of lower-fidelity models that provide partial but informative signals at substantially reduced cost. Multi-fidelity BO (MFBO) algorithms aim to strategically combine these information sources to achieve an optimal trade-off between accuracy and evaluation cost. However, existing MFBO methods often oversimplify the complex dependencies between fidelity levels or rely on heuristic acquisition functions that lack theoretical performance guarantees. To address these limitations, we introduce a new formulation of the MFBO problem as a fused Gaussian Process bandit and develop a corresponding Fused Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (FGP-UCB) algorithm. Our approach accurately predicts the high-fidelity function by fusing multi-fidelity observations through an autoregressive Gaussian Process model and explicitly quantifies the uncertainty arising from parameter estimation across fidelity levels. The proposed method also provides theoretical simple-regret guarantees, overcoming a key limitation of existing MFBO algorithms that lack provable performance bounds. Effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated via both theoretical analysis and empirical studies.

items.title: Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation
items.description: arXiv:2611.33080v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
items.description: arXiv:2611.33102v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived (rather than freshly generated) rollouts, but this generally leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy we call maximum likelihood replay: fitting the model to its archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood replay on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.

items.title: Dynamic Tensor Product Regression
items.description: arXiv:2210.03961v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we initiate the study of Dynamic Tensor Product Regression. One has matrices $A_1\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times d_1},\ldots,A_q\in \mathbb{R}^{n_q\times d_q}$ and a label vector $b\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\ldots n_q}$, and the goal is to solve the regression problem with the design matrix $A$ being the tensor product of the matrices $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_q$ i.e. $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1\ldots d_q}} \|(A_1\otimes \ldots\otimes A_q)x-b\|_2$. At each time step, one matrix $A_i$ receives a sparse change, and the goal is to maintain a sketch of the tensor product $A_1\otimes\ldots \otimes A_q$ so that the regression solution can be updated quickly. Recomputing the solution from scratch for each round is very slow and so it is important to develop algorithms which can quickly update the solution with the new design matrix. Our main result is a dynamic tree data structure where any update to a single matrix can be propagated quickly throughout the tree. We show that our data structure can be used to solve dynamic versions of not only Tensor Product Regression, but also Tensor Product Spline regression (which is a generalization of ridge regression) and for maintaining Low Rank Approximations for the tensor product.

items.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
items.description: arXiv:2310.10239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

items.title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
items.description: arXiv:2402.02552v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.

items.title: Point2SSM++: Self-Supervised Learning of Anatomical Shape Models from Point Clouds
items.description: arXiv:2405.09707v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Correspondence-based statistical shape modeling (SSM) stands as a powerful technology for morphometric analysis in clinical research. SSM facilitates population-level characterization and quantification of anatomical shapes such as bones and organs, aiding in pathology and disease diagnostics and treatment planning. Despite its potential, SSM remains under-utilized in medical research due to the significant overhead associated with automatic construction methods, which demand complete, aligned shape surface representations. Additionally, optimization-based techniques rely on bias-inducing assumptions or templates and have prolonged inference times as the entire cohort is simultaneously optimized. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Point2SSM++, a principled, self-supervised deep learning approach that directly learns correspondence points from point cloud representations of anatomical shapes. Point2SSM++ is robust to misaligned and inconsistent input, providing SSM that accurately samples individual shape surfaces while effectively capturing population-level statistics. Furthermore, we present extensions of Point2SSM++ tailored for dynamic spatiotemporal and multi-anatomy scenarios, showcasing the broad versatility of the framework. Through extensive validation across diverse anatomies, evaluation metrics, and clinically relevant downstream tasks, we demonstrate Point2SSM++'s superiority over existing state-of-the-art deep learning models and the traditional approach. Point2SSM++ substantially enhances the feasibility of SSM generation and significantly broadens its array of potential clinical applications.

items.title: ADformer: A Multi-Granularity Spatial-Temporal Transformer for EEG-Based Alzheimer Detection
items.description: arXiv:2409.00032v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electroencephalography has emerged as a cost-effective, efficient tool to help neurologists detect Alzheimer's Disease. However, most existing approaches rely heavily on manual feature engineering or data transformation. While these techniques may help with small-scale datasets, they often cause information loss and distortion when applied to large-scale data, ultimately limiting model performance. Moreover, the limited subject scale and demographic diversity of datasets used in prior studies hinder comprehensive evaluation of model robustness and generalizability, thus restricting their applicability in real-world clinical settings. To address these challenges, we propose ADformer, a novel multi-granularity spatial-temporal transformer that captures both temporal and spatial features from raw EEG signals, enabling effective end-to-end representation learning. Our model introduces multi-granularity embedding strategies across both spatial and temporal dimensions, leveraging a two-stage intra-inter-granularity self-attention mechanism to learn local patterns within each granularity and global dependencies across granularities. We evaluate ADformer on 4 large-scale datasets totaling 1,713 subjects, one of the largest corpora for EEG-based AD detection to date, under a cross-validated, subject-independent setting. Experimental results demonstrate that ADformer consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving subject-level F1 scores of 87.11%, 89.83%, 67.99%, and 84.42% on the 4 datasets, respectively, in distinguishing Alzheimer's Disease patients from healthy control subjects.

items.title: Protecting Confidentiality, Privacy and Integrity in Collaborative Learning
items.description: arXiv:2412.08534v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A collaboration between dataset owners and model owners is needed for effective machine learning (ML) training. During this collaboration, however, dataset owners and model owners want to protect the confidentiality of their respective assets (i.e., datasets, models and training code), with the dataset owners also caring about the privacy of individual users whose data is in the datasets. Existing solutions provide limited confidentiality for models and training code, suffer from data privacy issues, or incur unacceptable performance. We present Citadel++, a collaborative ML training system to simultaneously protect the confidentiality of datasets, models and training code as well as the privacy of individual user data. Specifically, Citadel++ takes a chained approach. First, we employ the Virtual Machine-level Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) as the training runtime to provide confidentiality protections for datasets, model and training code. Second, we create a privacy barrier that improves upon differential privacy techniques to safeguard the privacy of individual user data while maintaining model utility. Third, we construct and optimize a Virtual Machine Privilege Level (VMPL)-enforced fine-grained sandbox to regulate the dataflow in the system to ensure that our privacy barrier is always applied even when the model and training code maybe maliciously designed. Finally, we employ specific TEE capabilities to ensure the integrity of our privacy barrier and sandboxing mechanisms for their correct execution. To our knowledge, Citadel++ is the first collaborative training system providing strong confidentiality and privacy protections for dataset owners and model owners simultaneously. We analyze Citadel++ security properties and implement a full prototype. Our evaluation shows that Citadel++ provides strong guarantees with modest overheads.

items.title: DRAFT-ing Architectural Design Decisions using LLMs
items.description: arXiv:2504.08207v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Architectural Knowledge Management (AKM) is crucial for software development and Architectural Decision Records (ADR), an important artifact of AKM, provide a structured approach to capture Architectural Design Decisions (ADD). However, their adoption is limited due to the manual effort involved and insufficient tool support. Prior work shows that LLMs can support ADD generation, though basic prompting yields suboptimal results. This paper explores how LLMs can support architects in two complementary tasks: generating ADDs from Decision Contexts, and generating complete ADRs from titles. We propose Domain-specific Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Tuning (DRAFT), a novel approach that integrates Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Generation with Fine-tuning to generate. DRAFT operates in two phases: an offline phase that fine-tunes a model using retrieval-augmented prompts derived from historical ADRs, and an online phase that generates decisions or complete ADRs by combining retrieved examples with the fine-tuned model. Evaluated on 4344 ADRs across multiple LLMs using standard NLP metrics, DRAFT consistently produces outputs better aligned with real-world ADRs. A human evaluation with the authors and external architects, however, shows no uniformly preferred approach. DRAFT also maintains practical efficiency, reduces dependence- dence on proprietary models, and addresses organizational concerns around privacy, resource constraints, and inference costs.

items.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
items.description: arXiv:2504.08604v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning can seamlessly transfer agile locomotion and navigation skills from the simulator to real world. However, bridging the sim-to-real gap with domain randomization or adversarial methods often demands expert physics knowledge to ensure policy robustness. Even so, cutting-edge simulators may fall short of capturing every real-world detail, and the reconstructed environment may introduce errors due to various perception uncertainties. To address these challenges, we propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a novel framework that employs conditional score-based diffusion models to calibrate simulator physical coefficients and residual fidelity domains online during robot execution. Specifically, the residual fidelity reflects the simulation model shift relative to the real-world dynamics and captures the uncertainty of the perceived environment, enabling us to sample realistic environments under the inferred distribution for policy fine-tuning. Our framework is informative and adaptive in three key ways: (a) we fine-tune the pretrained policy only under anomalous scenarios, (b) we build sequential NFC online with the pretrained NFC's proposal prior, reducing the diffusion model's training burden, and (c) when NFC uncertainty is high and may degrade policy improvement, we leverage optimistic exploration to enable hallucinated policy optimization. Our framework achieves superior simulator calibration precision compared to state-of-the-art methods across diverse robots with high-dimensional parametric spaces. We study the critical contribution of residual fidelity to policy improvement in simulation and real-world experiments. Notably, our approach demonstrates robust robot navigation under challenging real-world conditions, such as a broken wheel axle on snowy surfaces.

items.title: A Unifying Framework for Robust and Efficient Inference with Unstructured Data
items.description: arXiv:2505.00282v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI can cheaply extract structured variables from unstructured data, with alternative implementation choices potentially yielding different measures of the same concept. This creates a credibility challenge, effectively moving specification search upstream.
